## Summary

**What a Kelvin wave is:** A Kelvin wave isn't a surface swell — it's a slow-moving, basin-wide pulse of water (or air) trapped along the equator or a coastline. An **equatorial Kelvin wave** forms when trade winds weaken/reverse, letting warm water normally piled up near Asia slosh eastward across the Pacific at 50–250 m depth over 2–3 months. When it hits South America, part of it turns and travels north as a **coastal Kelvin wave**, a band of slightly elevated sea level moving up the Americas at ~6 mph.

**The news:** A massive equatorial Kelvin wave (subsurface anomalies up to +8°C) has been feeding an exceptionally strong El Niño for winter 2026–27 (>90% chance of a very strong event per NOAA CPC). Its coastal branch is now working up the West Coast — expected in Southern California late Sept/early Oct, the Central Coast by mid-October, and San Francisco with roughly a foot of sea-level rise by mid-October. Forecasters warn the real danger is if this coincides with November–January king tides and winter storms.

**The visualization** (single HTML file, light/dark aware, colorblind-validated) includes: an explainer, 3 headline stat tiles, a schematic Pacific/Americas map showing both waves and city-by-city arrival dates, a timeline chart with a highlighted Nov–Jan flood-risk window, an illustrative subsurface-warming-by-depth chart, and a table view + sources.
